features.name: Names resolved at the operator's screen
features.description: The IPS dashboard receives only digital IDs. When the operator's session opens, it fetches names from the customer's own identity service using a signed token, and they are held in the browser for that session only. The vendor platform stores and logs digital IDs and nothing else.
features.hmw: How might we let an operator see who is where on the floor without the vendor's platform ever holding who that person is?

features.name: Live, fading and gone states on every marker
features.description: Each marker carries an explicit presence state with its last-seen age. It is live while readings arrive, fading after a defined silence, and removed at a defined timeout. Logout and a device switch skip straight to removal. The timings come from one agreed configuration rather than being implied.

design_directions.name: The trust boundary is the product boundary
design_directions.summary: Two products, split where the PII rule splits them. The IPS dashboard is an infrastructure console that shows anchors, the store computer and anonymous markers, and never a name. The customer-cloud dashboard, which already owns the identity mapping, is where people are seen by name. The integrator gets a health panel and a heartbeat so their side of the split is observable.
design_directions.differentiator: Identity never enters any surface the vendor runs, so PII safety is enforced by which product you are in, not by careful engineering inside one.
hmws_addressed: How might we let an operator see who is where on the floor without the vendor's platform ever holding who that person is?
How might we make it unmistakable whether a person on the map is present now, fading out of range, or already gone?
How might we give an operator confidence that changing a live anchor will not silently interrupt tracking for the people on it?
How might we let an integrator learn that the location stream or the SDK config feed has stopped before anyone on the floor notices tracking is gone?
design_directions.tradeoff: Two dashboards to build and keep consistent, and an operator who needs both 'is the anchor up' and 'who is near it' switches tools. DENSO's own demo of 'who is where' depends on the customer-side build being ready.

design_directions.name: One pane, names resolved at the glass
design_directions.summary: A single dashboard for everything: map, people, anchors, telemetry, configuration. The vendor platform holds digital IDs only. Names are fetched from the customer's identity service into the operator's browser per session, with pseudonymous markers and on-purpose reveals as the fallback. The operator's drill-down and change flows are built for confidence: one panel explains a reading, and a preview shows who a change will affect.
design_directions.differentiator: The operator works in one place and PII safety is an architectural guarantee inside it. It is the most direct reading of the RFQ's single-dashboard feature list.
hmws_addressed: How might we let an operator see who is where on the floor without the vendor's platform ever holding who that person is?
How might we make it unmistakable whether a person on the map is present now, fading out of range, or already gone?
How might we help an operator tell a bad reading for one person from a failing anchor before they act on either?
How might we give an operator confidence that changing a live anchor will not silently interrupt tracking for the people on it?
design_directions.tradeoff: The demo cannot show a single name until the customer exposes a signed identity-lookup endpoint, so it is gated on customer engineering. If that endpoint is down mid-demo, every marker falls back to an alias. Browser-side resolution is also harder to audit than a server-side split.

design_directions.name: The system watches itself
design_directions.summary: Automation first. The platform decides presence states, flags drifting anchors, stages and rolls back OTA updates, and emits a heartbeat so a silent stream raises an alarm. The operator handles exceptions and reads a timeline of what happened instead of watching a map for things going wrong.
design_directions.differentiator: It moves the work of noticing from the operator to the system, which fits an operations product better than a demo one.
hmws_addressed: How might we make it unmistakable whether a person on the map is present now, fading out of range, or already gone?
How might we help an operator tell a bad reading for one person from a failing anchor before they act on either?
How might we give an operator confidence that changing a live anchor will not silently interrupt tracking for the people on it?
How might we let an integrator learn that the location stream or the SDK config feed has stopped before anyone on the floor notices tracking is gone?
design_directions.tradeoff: It is the most effort (drift detection and staged OTA alone are about 5 person-months) and depends on store-computer and firmware behaviour this RFQ puts out of scope. False drift alarms would erode the trust it is meant to build. The RFQ still requires the raw telemetry views, so this adds to the operator surfaces rather than replacing them, and it leaves the identity conflict (HMW 1) unanswered.
